A cut-paper picture of five faceless men standing still side by side, all in profile and all facing right, each held in his own gesture, in front of a backdrop that steps down from lighter sheets on the left to bare background on the right. The one point of accent is a small bundle of scrolls that the man on the right holds out toward the empty space ahead of him.

The background is the first stack layer, the darkest sheet, flat and empty, and it fills the whole right half of the picture. The left half is built from three opaque backdrop sheets laid behind the figures, never in front of them, so the left side of the picture is lighter and the right side is the darkest. The five figures stand at even intervals across the middle of the picture, the left one centred about one sixth of the width in from the left edge and the right one a little short of three quarters of the way across. Every figure has both feet planted on the same level, a little above the bottom edge, with no leg in stride and no heel lifted: what changes from one figure to the next is posture, never a step. All five heads sit in the upper third of the picture. From just past the scrolls to the right edge there is nothing but bare background.

The focal point sits a little more than three quarters of the way across and just below mid-height: a bundle of five closed scrolls, offered with both hands toward the empty space on the right, where nobody stands. The bundle lies level across the old man's two upturned palms at chest height, its length pointing right, one hand under each end, never raised above the chest. Seen from the side it reads as five short straight bars stacked into one neat block, each scroll cut separately with thin gaps between them. Every scroll shows protruding roller ends just beyond the rolled paper at both ends, and a single cord ties the bundle round its middle; the roller ends and the cord are the secondary figure tone. The rolled paper itself is the accent: one flat solid tone with straight edges and no halo around it, and the only accent anywhere in the picture.

The man holding it is a stooped old man in the secondary figure tone, the lighter figure tone, standing against the darkest sheet, which makes him the figure with the strongest contrast in the picture. His back bends in three straight facets, his head is low and pushed forward, his knees are slightly bent and both feet are on the ground. He is shorter than the upright man to his left, yet his head still stays in the upper third. Nothing about him is triumphant.

The other four figures are the primary figure tone. On the far left, a boy raising a wooden sword: the smallest figure, leaning forward, both hands gripping a short practice sword lifted above his head almost vertically, kept inside his own column so it never reaches his neighbour or the left margin. Next to him stands a young man in plain, unmarked armor, the broadest and heaviest silhouette, rigid, feet set wide, arms held away from his body. A stepped armor outline does all the work: square shoulder guards and an armor skirt whose edges drop in straight steps like overlapping paper strips, and a low, plain helmet whose neck guard falls in steps. He stays one solid block of silhouette, with no plates drawn inside and no ornament on the helmet.

In the centre stands the tallest man, his head the highest in the picture. With both hands at one end he holds an extra-long wooden sword diagonally in front of his body, rising forward at 45 degrees: a straight, smooth, plain shaft with no metal tip, its far end cut off in a 45 degree chamfer. It is the longest blade in the picture, about twice the length of the boy's sword and longer than any scabbard, yet its tip stops in the gap before the next man without touching him.

To his right, a man nearing fifty stands upright and still, feet together. His two sheathed swords are thrust through the sash at his waist, hilts pointing forward in front of his belly, scabbard ends pointing back behind his hips. His arms hang loose at his sides and his hands are open and empty.

Behind the three left-hand figures, the three opaque backdrop sheets are anchored to the left edge and stacked one on top of another, each a step lighter than the sheet beneath it. Each runs the full height of the picture and ends in one straight vertical cut from top edge to bottom edge, and every cut falls exactly in the empty gap between two figures, never through one. The top sheet is the fourth stack layer, the lightest, and ends between the boy and the armored man. The middle sheet is the third stack layer and ends between the armored man and the tallest man. The bottom sheet is the second stack layer and ends between the tallest man and the man nearing fifty. The man nearing fifty and the old man stand against the bare first stack layer, with no sheet behind them. Because the sheet behind the boy is closest to his own tone, the boy almost sinks into it; each figure further right stands against a darker sheet and separates from it more clearly. The sheets are fully opaque and lie pressed flat on one another, with crisp edges and nothing cast between them.

The tallest man, the man nearing fifty and the old man each wear a trapezoid hakama in their own figure tone: wide pleated trousers that flare from the hips to the feet as a trapezoid of straight cuts, with two or three thin vertical slits marking the pleats. All five are flat paper silhouettes without faces: no eyes, no features, no lines drawn inside the shapes.

The only vertical edges between the figures are the three sheet cuts: no borders, boxes or dividing lines, no ruler or tick marks.

Nothing in the image is readable. The scrolls are closed and bare on the outside, with no marks, no characters and no seal. No letters, words, numerals or characters of any script, real or invented, anywhere, not even small or decorative ones. The background stays empty: no sun disc, no branches or blossoms, no mountains, no waves, no gates.
